extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and TeX users typesetting mathematical formulas (people learning plain TeX math conventions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and low-level rules for choosing, sizing, and implementing delimiters and related math constructs in plain TeX; includes font family, mathcode, and delimiter encoding conventions. Intended to teach how to produce visually correct mathematical formulas with TeX primitives and macros.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: Delimiters provide good visual clues to the underlying structure of complex expressions: they delimit the boundaries of individual subformulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose delimiters to make the structure of nested formulas clear; the book lists the 22 basic delimiters provided by plain TeX as the canonical set to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic set of 22 delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX supplies 22 basic delimiter symbols (parentheses, brackets, braces, floor/ceiling, angle brackets, slash/backslash, vertical bars, arrows, up/down arrows, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided control sequences (e.g. \lfloor/\rfloor, \langle/\rangle, \vert/\Vert) rather than attempting unavailable keyboard characters; the text gives explicit mappings and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not type literal braces for delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: You should never try to specify a left brace or right brace simply by typing '{' or '}', because '{' and '}' are reserved for grouping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use control sequences such as \lbrace and \rbrace (or \{ and \}) to get brace delimiters. Typing raw '{' or '}' will perform grouping rather than produce brace symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual delimiter sizing commands (\big, \Big, \bigg, \Bigg)
rubrics_metrics.description: Preceding a delimiter by \bigl/\bigr (opening/closing) gives a slightly larger delimiter; \Bigl/\Bigr produce larger symbols, \biggl/\biggr and \Biggl/\Biggr produce still larger ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \big*/\Big*/\bigg*/\Bigg* variants when you want specific visible size differences (examples in text show ordinary vs \big vs \Big vs \biggl vs \Biggl). These are useful inside text or displays depending on required height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Middle delimiters (\bigm, \Bigm, \biggm, \Biggm)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides \bigm and variants for delimiters used in the middle of formulas; such a delimiter acts like a relation and TeX inserts spacing on either side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \bigm when the delimiter should behave like a relation (e.g. between sets or expressions) so TeX applies relation spacing. Example: \bigcup_n X_n \bigm\{ \bigcap_n Y_n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of bare \big / \Big without l/m/r suffix
rubrics_metrics.description: Saying just \big or \Big (no l/m/r suffix) produces a delimiter that acts as an ordinary variable; used primarily with slashes and backslashes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form is useful when you want a delimiter that does not act as opening/closing/middle; example: fraction-with-slash usage: {a+1\over b}\bigg/ {c+1\over d}.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic sizing with \left and \right
rubrics_metrics.description: \left and \right tell TeX to compute how tall delimiters must be to enclose the enclosed subformula; TeX chooses a delimiter size just big enough to cover the subformula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \left( ... \right) to let TeX pick delimiter sizes. Remember that \left and \right also act as grouping: they must pair within the same formula and cannot cross grouping boundaries or be split across formulas or groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pairing and grouping behavior of \left and \right
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever you use \left and \right they must pair up with each other (like braces). You cannot have \left in one formula and \right in another, nor cross groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because TeX must typeset the enclosed subformula to decide delimiter size, \left and \right must appear in the same formula and not be separated by group boundaries (e.g. \begingroup/\endgroup). However, when not using \left/\right, TeX allows unbalanced delimiters like '[0,1)' without complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three situations requiring manual delimiter sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: There are at least three situations when you will want to choose delimiter sizes manually rather than relying on \left/\right: (1) \left/\right choose a smaller delimiter than desired; (2) they choose a larger delimiter than desired (e.g. enclosing a large operator with limits); (3) when breaking a huge displayed formula across lines and you need opening and closing delimiters to have the same size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \big*/\Big*/\bigg*/\Biggl etc. in those cases; e.g. use \biggl around a \sum so limits 'hang out', or use explicit \Biggl/\Biggr on separate lines to ensure identical sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Null delimiter (invisible counterpart)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you type '.' (a period) after \left or \right instead of specifying a basic delimiter you get a null delimiter (blank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Null delimiters are useful when you need only one visible delimiter (for example piecewise definitions: |x| = \left\{ ... \right.). A null delimiter is an empty box with width given by \nulldelimiterspace (plain TeX sets it to 1.2pt).

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle bracket abbreviations in delimiter context
rubrics_metrics.description: You can type '<' or '>' as convenient abbreviations for \langle and \rangle when TeX is looking for a delimiter; ordinarily '<' and '>' are less-than and greater-than relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use '<' and '>' only when TeX is in a delimiter-expecting context (e.g. after \bigl or \left); otherwise they produce relational symbols, which are different from angle brackets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special repeatable-part delimiters (\arrowvert, \Arrowvert, \bracevert, \lgroup/\rgroup, \lmoustache/\rmoustache)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX provides special delimiters built from repeatable parts of vertical arrows, double vertical arrows, and large braces, as well as \lgroup/\rgroup (constructed from braces without the middle parts) and half-moustaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These produce delimiters with different weight/whitespace. \lgroup and \rgroup look like bold parentheses but are available only in large sizes (\Big or more), so they cannot be used exactly like ordinary parentheses in all contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscript/superscript scoping differences with delimiters
rubrics_metrics.description: A subscript or superscript following a large delimiter behaves differently depending on whether the delimiter was produced by \left/\right or by \big*/\bigr etc.: after a \left delimiter it is the first sub/superscript of the enclosed subformula (effectively preceded by {}), after a \right delimiter it is a sub/superscript of the entire \left...\right subformula, and after \bigl/\bigr it applies only to that particular delimiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that :\bigl(_2) and :\left(_2) have different effects; choose delimiter form based on desired attachment of scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axis centering and delimiter geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Large parentheses and brackets are symmetric with respect to an invisible horizontal line called the axis (a little above the baseline); when a delimiter grows its height and depth both increase by the same amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axis is the reference for vertical centering: fraction bar lines are centered on the axis regardless of numerator/denominator size. Use \vcenter{...} to create boxes centered on the axis when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of \vcenter for vertical centering in math mode
rubrics_metrics.description: \vcenter{(vertical mode material)} packs material into a box and raises/lowers it so its top edge is as far above the axis as its bottom edge is below, making it vertically centered with respect to the math axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \vcenter is only meaningful in math mode; to center something vertically in horizontal mode you can use $\vcenter{...}$. Variants like \vcenter to(dimen) and \vcenter spread(dimen) are legal too.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining style-dependent symbols with \mathchoice (costly)
rubrics_metrics.description: \mathchoice{(math)}{(math)}{(math)}{(math)} selects among four subformulas for display/text/script/scriptscript styles; TeX actually typesets all four before choosing the final one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \mathchoice when you need different constructions in different styles (display vs text vs script vs scriptscript), but note \mathchoice is expensive in time and space because TeX typesets all variants — use sparingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Macro helper \mathpalette
rubrics_metrics.description: \mathpalette provides a convenient way to write macros that need to adapt to the current math style: \mathpalette\a{xyz} expands to the fourfold array \mathchoice{\a\displaystyle{xyz}}... etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \mathpalette when implementing \mathchoice-like behavior; Appendix B contains examples (definitions of \phantom, \root, \smash and constructions for congruence sign use it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalized fraction primitives (\overwithdelims, \atopwithdelims, \abovewithdelims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primitives \overwithdelims{delim1}{delim2}, \atopwithdelims{...}{...}, and \abovewithdelims{...}{...}{dimen} form the generalized-fraction feature: they place numerator over denominator with enclosing delimiters and allow explicit bar thickness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: \abovewithdelims is the most general (explicit thickness); \over and \atop are special cases with null delimiters; delimiters placed depend on surrounding style not fraction style (e.g. \choose is equivalent to \atopwithdelims 0 0). Examples: defining Legendre symbol or Eulerian number via these primitives.

rubrics_metrics.name: When \left/\right choose delimiter sizes (calculation parameters)
rubrics_metrics.description: Appendix G explains TeX computes desired size: delimiters are vertically centered with respect to the axis; if a subformula extends h1 above and h2 below, needed size is at least 2*max(h1,h2). TeX allows parameters \delimiterfactor f and \delimitershortfall J to adjust sizing; Appendix B sets f=901 and J=5pt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimum delimiter size is taken to be at least max(2*max(h1,h2), (2*max...) * f/1000, and at least 2*max(h1,h2) - J). These parameters can be set if you are designing formats; default values give slightly smaller than full coverage to look better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Math character classes and codes (classes 0–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every math character has a class number 0–7 indicating its 'part of speech' in math: 0 ordinary, 1 large operator, 2 binary operation, 3 relation, 4 opening, 5 closing, 6 punctuation, 7 variable-family special case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Class number is combined with family and position into hexadecimal mathchar codes (e.g. \sum = "1350 means class 1/operator in family 3 position 50). Class 7 characters use the current \fam value to determine family, making letters convenient in math mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modifying interpretation via \mathcode and \mathchar/\mathchardef
rubrics_metrics.description: TeX looks up math behavior in the mathcode table (256 entries). You can change entries with \mathcode to treat characters differently (e.g. make '<' a relation via \mathcode'<=...). Use \mathchar to specify character codes directly and \mathchardef to define control sequences as math characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial setups: INITEX sets defaults; ten digits and letters have special initial mathcodes. Use \mathcode for remapping single characters; \mathchardef is convenient for defining many special symbol macros as in Appendix B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class 7 (variable-family) and \fam behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Class 7 behaves like class 0 unless \fam has been set to a legal family (0–15); INITEX sets \fam=-1 on entering math mode so class 7 equals class 0 by default. Plain TeX uses macros like \rm to set \fam=0 and make letters become roman in formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \fam changes (via \rm or macros) to switch which family letters belong to in math mode (e.g. to get bold math italics, define \bmit as \fam=9).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delimiter codes (\delcode) — small and large variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Each character has a \delcode giving either negative (not a delimiter) or a six-hex-digit code: the first three digits specify the 'small' variant and the last three the 'large' variant. TeX checks the \delcode when a character follows \left or \right or a withdelims command, tries small then large variant; negative \delcode yields error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \delcode'(<value>) to set mapping (Appendix B examples: \delcode'('=11 028300 specifies small variant etc.). If a variant is 000 it is ignored. All \delcode values are -1 until changed. Appendix G discusses how fonts supply linked larger variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct numeric \delimiter primitive
rubrics_metrics.description: A delimiter can be given directly as \delimiter<number> where the number is up to seven hex digits: the leading digit is class (0–7) and the remaining digits encode small/large variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When \delimiter appears after \left or \right the class digit is ignored; in other contexts (not looking for a delimiter) the three rightmost digits are dropped and the remaining four act as a \mathchar. Example: \def\langle{\delimiter 11 426830A} defines an opening with small variant "268 and large "30A. Beware of wrong placements such as \bigl \delimiter... which are incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radical and mathaccent low-level primitives
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX defines \sqrt via a \radical primitive and \widehat via \mathaccent so TeX knows the family and positions of the symbols used in radical and accent constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These low-level numeric conventions pack information compactly and allow TeX to position radicals/accents precisely; Appendix G gives precise positioning rules. Redefinition allows different radical styles when fonts supply necessary symbols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Font families for math and required fontdimen parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Plain TeX assigns family 1 to math italic letters, family 2 to ordinary math symbols, and family 3 to large symbols. Families 2 and 3 must have special \fontdimen parameters that govern mathematical spacing (cmsy and cmex have these parameters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Family assignments can be changed and \newfam creates new family names; however, fonts used in families 2 and 3 must supply the needed parameters or spacing rules won't behave properly. Use \fontdimen to modify parameters if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of font assignments inside formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: While a formula is being read TeX remembers each symbol's class/family/position but does not take note of what fonts are actually in the families until reaching the end of the formula. Thus changes to \textfontN mid-formula will affect final font selection only at the end, unless the subformula is typeset early (e.g. inside an \hbox).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: $\textfont0=\tenrm 9 \textfont0=\Helvetica 9$ results in both 9s from \Helvetica (final setting), whereas $\textfont0=\tenrm 9 \hbox{$9\textfont0=\Helvetica$}$ yields first 9 from \tenrm and second from \Helvetica because the hbox was typeset before incorporation.
